BMA-05.Change log: A record of every requested change to the project's scope, schedule or budget and whether each was approved.
BMA-05.Stakeholder register: A list of the people and groups affected by the project, with their interests, influence and what they need to be told.
BMA-05.Lessons learned report: A document written at the end of a project recording what went well and what went badly, so future projects can do better.
BMA-05.Burndown chart: A graph, used in agile projects, that plots the work remaining against time and should slope down to zero by the deadline.
BMA-05.Earned value analysis: A method that compares the value of the work actually completed with the planned schedule and the money spent, to show if a project is behind or over budget.

ECO-04.Public schools: Free schooling from kindergarten through 12th grade, paid for mostly with state and local taxes such as property tax.
ECO-04.Roads: Streets, highways and bridges that governments build and maintain so that people and goods can move around.
ECO-04.Police: Officers employed by local, state and federal government to enforce the law and keep people and property safe.
ECO-04.Fire protection: Fire departments that put out fires and respond to rescues, usually run and funded by local government.
ECO-04.National defense: The armed forces that protect the country. It is a classic public good: everyone is protected whether or not they pay.
ECO-04.Parks: Public land set aside for recreation and nature, from neighborhood playgrounds to national parks.
ECO-04.Libraries: Public buildings where anyone can borrow books and use computers and other resources at no charge, funded mainly by local taxes.
ECO-04.Public transportation: Buses, subways and trains run or subsidized by government, with fares that usually cover only part of the cost.
ECO-04.Social Security: A federal program, funded by payroll taxes, that pays monthly income to retired workers, disabled workers and survivors of workers who have died.
ECO-04.Health programs: Government health coverage and services, such as Medicare for older Americans and Medicaid for people with low incomes.
ECO-04.Courts: The system of judges and courtrooms that tries criminal cases and settles legal disputes, including business disputes.
ECO-04.Prisons: Jails and prisons where people convicted of crimes, or awaiting trial, are held at public expense.
ECO-04.Water and sewer service: Local systems that supply clean drinking water and carry away and treat wastewater. Users often pay fees as well as taxes.
ECO-04.Public assistance: Programs that help people with low incomes pay for basics, such as food benefits, housing aid and cash assistance.
ECO-04.Public colleges and student aid: State universities and community colleges supported by tax money, plus government grants and loans that help students pay for college.
ECO-04.Postal service: Mail delivery to every address in the country. The U.S. Postal Service is a government agency, though it is funded mostly by postage, not taxes.
ECO-04.Emergency services: Help in urgent situations, such as 911 call centers, ambulances and disaster relief after storms and floods.
ECO-04.Street lighting: Lights along public roads. They are a public good, since everyone passing benefits and no one can be charged per use.
ECO-04.Veterans benefits: Health care, education funding, pensions and other support the government gives to people who served in the military.
ECO-04.Environmental protection: Government work to limit pollution, clean up contaminated sites and conserve land and wildlife.
ECO-04.Scientific research: Government funding for science, medicine and space exploration, which private firms may not pay for because the payoff is uncertain or far off.
ECO-04.Foreign aid: Money, food and other help that a government gives to other countries for development, disaster relief or security.
ECO-04.Farm subsidies: Government payments to farmers that support their incomes and help steady the supply and price of crops.
ECO-04.Public broadcasting: Noncommercial television and radio, such as PBS and NPR stations, which have long relied on government funds for part of their budgets.
ECO-04.Elections: Running elections, including registering voters, staffing polling places and counting ballots, is paid for by government.
ECO-04.Food and drug safety: Government inspection and approval of food, medicines and restaurants to make sure they are safe for the public.
ECO-04.Weather service: The National Weather Service gathers weather data and issues forecasts and storm warnings for the public at no charge.
ECO-04.Museums: Public museums and arts programs, such as the Smithsonian, that are supported partly or wholly with tax money.

ECO-05.Tariff: A tax on imported goods. It raises the price of foreign products so that domestic ones are more competitive.
ECO-05.Quota: A limit on the quantity or value of a product that can be imported during a set period.
ECO-05.Embargo: A government order that bans trade with a particular country, or in a particular product, usually for political reasons.
ECO-05.Sanctions: Penalties one country places on another to pressure it to change its behavior, such as limits on trade or on financial dealings.
ECO-05.Subsidies: Government payments to domestic producers that lower their costs, letting them sell for less than foreign competitors.
ECO-05.Import licenses: Permits that a business must get from the government before bringing certain goods into the country. Limiting them limits imports.
ECO-05.Product standards: Rules on safety, health, quality or labeling that imported goods must meet. Strict or unusual rules can keep foreign products out.
ECO-05.Currency controls: Government limits on how much foreign currency people and businesses can buy or sell, which makes it harder to pay for imports.
ECO-05.Anti-dumping or countervailing duties: Extra import taxes. Anti-dumping duties hit imports priced below their fair value. Countervailing duties offset subsidies from a foreign government.
ECO-05.Customs procedures: Paperwork, inspections and delays at the border that make importing slower and more costly. Often called red tape.
ECO-05.Currency devaluation: A government lowers the value of its currency, which makes its exports cheaper abroad and imports more expensive at home.
ECO-05.Export controls: Limits or bans a government places on selling certain goods to other countries, such as weapons or advanced technology.
ECO-05.Boycott: An organized refusal to buy goods from a particular country or company, used to apply pressure.
ECO-05.Local content requirements: Rules that a set share of a product must be made with domestic parts or labor for it to be sold or to avoid tariffs.
ECO-05.Voluntary export restraint: An agreement in which an exporting country limits how much it ships to another country, usually to avoid tougher barriers there.
ECO-05.Buy-national policies: Rules that government agencies must favor domestically made goods when they buy, such as Buy American laws.
ECO-05.Foreign ownership restrictions: Limits on how much of a domestic company or industry foreign investors may own, which keep foreign firms from setting up freely.
ECO-05.Quarantine rules: Health rules that hold, inspect or bar imported plants, animals and food to keep out pests and diseases, which also slow or block trade.

ECO-06.Consumer income: A demand shifter. When people earn more they buy more of most goods at every price, and when incomes fall they buy less.
ECO-06.Consumer tastes: A demand shifter. When a product becomes more popular or fashionable, people want more of it at every price.
ECO-06.Cost of inputs: A supply shifter. When materials, labor or energy cost more, producers offer less at each price, and when they cost less, producers offer more.
ECO-06.Price of substitutes: A demand shifter. If a product that can replace this one gets more expensive, buyers switch and demand for this one rises.
ECO-06.Price of complements: A demand shifter. Complements are used together, like printers and ink, so a higher price for one lowers demand for the other.
ECO-06.Number of buyers: A demand shifter. More consumers in a market, for example through population growth, means more is demanded at every price.
ECO-06.Technology: A supply shifter. Better technology lets producers make more at lower cost, so they supply more at every price.
ECO-06.Expectations: Shifts both curves. Buyers who expect prices to rise buy more now, and sellers who expect higher prices may hold goods back for later.
ECO-06.Number of sellers: A supply shifter. When more firms enter a market, more is offered for sale at every price.
ECO-06.Taxes: Mainly a supply shifter. A tax on producers raises their costs and cuts supply. Taxes that reduce take-home pay can also lower demand.
ECO-06.Advertising: A demand shifter. Successful advertising makes more people want a product at every price.
ECO-06.Subsidies: A supply shifter. A government payment to producers lowers their costs, so they supply more at every price.
ECO-06.Government regulations: Mainly a supply shifter. Rules that make production more costly reduce supply, and rules that restrict a product's use can cut demand.
ECO-06.Weather: Shifts both curves. Droughts and storms cut the supply of crops, and the season changes demand for goods such as coats or ice cream.
ECO-06.Availability of resources: A supply shifter. When the materials needed for production become scarce, producers cannot supply as much at any price.
ECO-06.Prices of alternative products: A supply shifter. If another good the producer could make becomes more profitable, the producer switches to it and supplies less of this one.
ECO-06.Availability of credit: A demand shifter. When loans are easy to get and interest rates are low, people buy more costly items such as cars and homes.
ECO-06.Tariffs and trade policy: A supply shifter. Tariffs and quotas raise the cost or limit the quantity of imports, which reduces supply in the home market.

BA-04.Spreadsheet: A program such as Excel that arranges numbers in rows and columns and does calculations, used for budgets, lists and analysis.
BA-04.Email: A system for sending written messages and files electronically, used for most day-to-day business communication.
BA-04.Word processing: Software such as Microsoft Word or Google Docs for writing, editing and formatting letters, reports and other documents.
BA-04.Accounting software: A program such as QuickBooks that records sales, expenses and payments and produces the financial statements.
BA-04.Database: An organized collection of records, such as customers or products, stored so that it can be searched, sorted and updated quickly.
BA-04.Presentation software: A program such as PowerPoint or Google Slides for building slides to show during a talk or meeting.
BA-04.Point-of-sale system: The checkout hardware and software that rings up sales, takes payment and records each transaction as it happens. Known as POS.
BA-04.Customer relationship management: Software that stores every customer's contact details, purchases and conversations so that sales and service staff can manage the relationship. Known as CRM.
BA-04.Video conferencing: Software such as Zoom that lets people in different places meet face to face over the internet with live video and sound.
BA-04.Messaging and collaboration software: Tools such as Slack or Microsoft Teams that let coworkers chat, share files and work together in real time.
BA-04.Project management software: A program such as Trello or Asana that tracks a project's tasks, deadlines and who is responsible for each.
BA-04.Payroll or HR system: A payroll system calculates pay, taxes and deductions and issues paychecks. A human resources system stores employee records, hours and benefits.
BA-04.Inventory management system: Software that tracks how much of each item is in stock, where it is and when more needs to be ordered.
BA-04.Cloud storage: Storing files on a provider's remote servers over the internet, as with Google Drive or Dropbox, so they can be reached from anywhere.
BA-04.Scheduling software: A program for setting up employee shifts or booking customer appointments and reservations.
BA-04.Security software: Programs such as antivirus tools and firewalls that protect computers and networks from viruses, hackers and data theft.
BA-04.Website: The company's pages on the internet, which give customers information and can also take orders and inquiries.
BA-04.Enterprise resource planning: One integrated system that links finance, inventory, production, sales and human resources through a shared database. Known as ERP.
BA-04.E-commerce platform: Software such as Shopify that runs an online store, with product pages, a shopping cart and checkout.
BA-04.Email marketing software: A tool such as Mailchimp for sending promotional emails to lists of customers and tracking who opens and clicks them.
BA-04.Data analytics software: Tools such as Tableau that turn large amounts of raw data into charts and dashboards, helping managers spot patterns. Often called business intelligence.
BA-04.Supply chain management system: Software that tracks and coordinates the flow of materials and products from suppliers through production to customers.
BA-04.Design software: Programs for creating graphics, page layouts or technical drawings, such as Photoshop or computer-aided design (CAD) tools.
BA-04.Operating system: The basic software, such as Windows or macOS, that runs a computer and lets all the other programs work.
BA-04.Payment processing system: A service such as Stripe or PayPal that moves a customer's card or online payment securely into the business's bank account.
BA-04.Management information system: A system that turns the company's routine data into regular summary reports that managers use to monitor and control operations. Known as MIS.
BA-04.Decision support system: A system that lets managers analyze data and test what-if scenarios to help with complex, non-routine decisions.
BA-04.Transaction processing system: A system that records the routine daily transactions of a business, such as sales, orders, payments and payroll.
BA-04.Electronic data interchange: The computer-to-computer exchange of standard business documents, such as purchase orders and invoices, between companies. Known as EDI.
BA-04.Help desk software: A system that logs each customer or employee request for support as a ticket and tracks it until it is solved.
BA-04.Material requirements planning: A system that uses the production schedule to work out which materials and parts to order and when. Known as MRP.
BA-04.Knowledge management system: A system for collecting and sharing what the company's people know, such as guides, answers and best practices, so others can find it.
BA-04.Artificial intelligence tools: Software that carries out tasks that normally need human thinking, such as writing drafts, answering questions or spotting patterns in data.
BA-04.Electronic signature software: A tool such as DocuSign that lets people sign contracts and forms on screen, so documents need not be printed and mailed.

POB-05.False advertising: Making untrue or misleading claims about a product in order to get people to buy it. It is illegal under federal and state law.
POB-05.Fraud: Deliberately deceiving someone for financial gain, such as falsifying the company's financial records or running a scam.
POB-05.Bribery: Offering money or gifts to someone in a position of power in exchange for a favorable decision, such as a contract.
POB-05.Discrimination or harassment: Discrimination is treating people unfairly at work because of traits such as race, sex or age. Harassment is unwelcome conduct that makes the workplace hostile.
POB-05.Embezzlement: Theft of money or property by a person who was trusted to look after it, such as an employee taking company funds.
POB-05.Insider trading: Buying or selling a company's stock using important information that has not been made public. It is illegal because other investors cannot compete fairly.
POB-05.Price fixing: Competitors secretly agreeing on what prices to charge instead of competing. It is illegal under antitrust law.
POB-05.Worker exploitation: Taking unfair advantage of workers, for example through child labor, pay below the legal minimum, unpaid overtime or unsafe conditions.
POB-05.Monopolizing: Using unfair tactics to gain or keep control of a market and shut out competitors, which antitrust law forbids.
POB-05.Tax evasion: Illegally avoiding taxes by hiding income or lying on tax returns. It differs from legal tax planning.
POB-05.Illegal dumping: Getting rid of waste, especially hazardous waste, in places or ways the law does not allow, to avoid the cost of proper disposal.
POB-05.Bait and switch: Advertising a product at a very low price to draw customers in, then pushing them to buy a more expensive one instead.
POB-05.Selling unsafe products: Knowingly selling goods that are defective or dangerous, or hiding a known defect from buyers.
POB-05.Privacy violations: Collecting, using or selling customers' personal information without their knowledge or permission.
POB-05.Money laundering: Hiding the source of money gained from crime by passing it through legitimate-looking businesses or accounts.
POB-05.Price gouging: Raising prices to unfairly high levels during an emergency, when people badly need items such as water or fuel. Many states outlaw it.
POB-05.Conflict of interest: A situation in which a person's private interests could sway decisions made for the company, such as awarding a contract to a relative.
POB-05.Intellectual property theft: Using or copying someone else's protected work without permission, such as pirating software, counterfeiting brands or stealing a trade secret.
POB-05.Corporate espionage: Spying on a competitor to steal confidential information, such as product designs or customer lists.
POB-05.Retaliation against whistleblowers: Punishing an employee, for example by firing or demoting, for reporting wrongdoing inside the company.
POB-05.Breach of contract: Failing, without a legal excuse, to do what was promised in a contract. It is a civil wrong that the other party can sue over.
POB-05.High-pressure sales tactics: Pushing or misleading customers into buying something they do not need or cannot afford, without giving them time to think.
POB-05.Greenwashing: Making a company or product seem more environmentally friendly than it really is.
POB-05.Planned obsolescence: Deliberately designing a product to wear out or go out of date quickly so customers must buy a replacement. Critics see it as unethical, though it is usually legal.
POB-05.Dumping goods below cost: Selling products in a foreign market below cost or below the home price in order to drive out local competitors.
POB-05.Tying arrangements: Forcing a customer who wants one product to buy a second product too. It can break antitrust law when the seller has market power.
POB-05.Padding expense accounts: Claiming repayment for business expenses that are inflated or were never actually spent.
POB-05.Market manipulation: Artificially pushing a stock's price up or down to mislead other investors, for example by spreading false information.
POB-05.Slander of competitors: Making false statements that damage a rival business's reputation or products.
POB-05.Deceptive packaging: Packaging that misleads the buyer, such as a large box that is mostly empty space, called slack fill.
POB-05.Redlining: Refusing loans, insurance or other services to people because of the neighborhood they live in, often on the basis of race. It is illegal.

LAW-04.Occupational Safety and Health Act: A 1970 law requiring employers to provide a workplace free from recognized serious hazards. It created the agency known as OSHA to set and enforce safety standards.
LAW-04.Civil Rights Act: The 1964 law whose Title VII bans employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin.
LAW-04.Americans with Disabilities Act: A 1990 law that bans discrimination against qualified workers with disabilities and requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for them.
LAW-04.Fair Labor Standards Act: A 1938 law that sets the federal minimum wage, requires overtime pay for most workers after 40 hours in a week and restricts child labor.
LAW-04.Family and Medical Leave Act: A 1993 law that gives eligible workers at larger employers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for a new child or a serious health condition.
LAW-04.Equal Pay Act: A 1963 law requiring that men and women be paid the same for substantially equal work in the same workplace.
LAW-04.Social Security Act: The 1935 law that created retirement benefits for workers, funded by payroll taxes, and set up the unemployment insurance system.
LAW-04.Age Discrimination in Employment Act: A 1967 law that protects workers aged 40 and over from discrimination in hiring, firing, pay and promotion because of their age.
LAW-04.National Labor Relations Act: A 1935 law, also called the Wagner Act, that gives private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively with employers.
LAW-04.Whistleblower Protection Act: A 1989 law that protects federal government employees from punishment for reporting waste, fraud or lawbreaking. Other laws give similar protection to private-sector workers.
LAW-04.COBRA: The Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act. It lets workers who lose or leave a job keep their employer's group health coverage for a time by paying the cost themselves.
LAW-04.ERISA: The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. It sets rules for private employers' pension and health plans to protect the benefits workers have been promised.
LAW-04.Pregnancy Discrimination Act: A 1978 law that makes it illegal to treat a worker unfavorably because of pregnancy, childbirth or a related medical condition.
LAW-04.Taft-Hartley Act: A 1947 law that limits union power. It bans closed shops and unfair practices by unions, and lets states pass right-to-work laws so workers cannot be forced to join.
LAW-04.Immigration Reform and Control Act: A 1986 law that requires employers to verify that new hires may legally work, and bars discrimination based on national origin or citizenship status.
LAW-04.Rehabilitation Act: A 1973 law that bans discrimination against people with disabilities by federal agencies, federal contractors and programs that receive federal money.
LAW-04.WARN Act: The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. It requires employers with 100 or more workers to give 60 days notice of a plant closing or mass layoff.
LAW-04.Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Ac: A 2008 law that bars employers from using genetic test results or family medical history in hiring, firing or other job decisions.
LAW-04.USERRA: The Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. It protects the civilian jobs of people who leave to serve in the military and bans bias against them.
LAW-04.Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act: A 2009 law that restarts the deadline for filing a pay discrimination claim with each unfair paycheck, so workers who learn of it late can still sue.
LAW-04.Employee Polygraph Protection Act: A 1988 law that stops most private employers from using lie detector tests to screen job applicants or to test employees.
LAW-04.Pregnant Workers Fairness Act: A law in effect since 2023 that requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for limitations related to pregnancy and childbirth.
LAW-04.Landrum-Griffin Act: A 1959 law that protects union members from abuses by their own unions, with a bill of rights for members and required financial reports.
LAW-04.Davis-Bacon Act: A 1931 law requiring that workers on federally funded construction projects be paid at least the local prevailing wage.
LAW-04.Norris-LaGuardia Act: A 1932 law that limits federal courts from issuing orders to stop peaceful strikes and makes contracts forbidding union membership unenforceable.
LAW-04.Federal Employees Compensation Act: A law that provides workers compensation, meaning medical care and wage replacement, to federal civilian employees injured on the job.
LAW-04.Mine Safety and Health Act: A 1977 law that sets safety and health standards for mines and requires regular federal inspections of them.
LAW-04.Consumer Credit Protection Act: A 1968 law that, for workers, limits how much of a paycheck can be taken to pay a debt and bars firing someone because of a single garnishment.
LAW-04.Walsh-Healey Act: A 1936 law that sets minimum wage, overtime and safety standards for workers on federal government contracts to make or supply goods.
LAW-04.Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker: A 1983 law that sets standards for the pay, housing, transport and record keeping of migrant and seasonal farmworkers.
LAW-04.PUMP Act: A 2022 law requiring employers to give nursing mothers break time and a private space, other than a bathroom, to express breast milk at work.

LAW-05.Negligence: Failing to use the care a reasonable person would use in the same situation, and so causing harm to someone else.
LAW-05.Defamation: Making a false statement of fact to others that harms a person's or a business's reputation. Libel and slander are its two forms.
LAW-05.Fraud: Intentionally misstating or hiding an important fact so that another person relies on it and suffers a loss.
LAW-05.Assault: An intentional act that makes another person reasonably fear immediate harmful contact. No touching is needed.
LAW-05.Battery: Intentional harmful or offensive physical contact with another person without that person's consent.
LAW-05.Libel: Defamation in a fixed form, such as writing, print, pictures or an online post.
LAW-05.Slander: Defamation that is spoken: a false oral statement that damages someone's reputation.
LAW-05.Trespass: Entering or staying on another person's land without permission or a legal right.
LAW-05.Product liability: The legal responsibility of makers and sellers for injuries caused by a defective or unreasonably dangerous product.
LAW-05.Strict liability: Legal responsibility for harm even when the defendant was not careless or at fault. It applies to abnormally dangerous activities and defective products.
LAW-05.Invasion of privacy: Wrongfully intruding into a person's private life, for example by spying on them or publicizing private facts.
LAW-05.Malpractice: Negligence by a professional, such as a doctor, lawyer or accountant, who fails to meet the standard of care of the profession.
LAW-05.Wrongful death: A claim brought by the family of a person who died because of someone else's negligence or wrongful act.
LAW-05.Premises liability: A property owner's responsibility for injuries caused by unsafe conditions on the property, such as a wet floor in a store.
LAW-05.False imprisonment: Intentionally confining or holding a person against their will without legal justification, such as a store wrongly detaining a shopper.
LAW-05.Nuisance: An unreasonable interference with other people's use and enjoyment of their property, such as constant noise, smoke or smells.
LAW-05.Intentional infliction of emotional dist: Extreme and outrageous conduct that is meant to cause, and does cause, severe emotional suffering to another person.
LAW-05.Theft of trade secrets: Taking or using another company's confidential business information, such as a formula or customer list, by improper means.
LAW-05.Wrongful termination: Firing an employee for an illegal reason, such as discrimination or revenge for reporting wrongdoing. Some states treat certain cases as a tort.
LAW-05.Infringement: Using someone's patent, copyright or trademark without permission. The owner can sue for damages.
LAW-05.Conversion: Wrongfully taking or keeping another person's personal property and treating it as your own. It is the civil counterpart of theft.
LAW-05.Interference with a contract: Intentionally causing one party to break a valid contract with another, for example by luring a supplier away from a rival.
LAW-05.Trespass to chattels: Intentionally interfering with another person's use of their movable personal property, such as borrowing or damaging it without permission.
LAW-05.Malicious prosecution: Bringing a baseless legal case against someone out of spite or for an improper purpose. The victim can sue once that case has ended in the victim's favor.
LAW-05.Disparagement: Making false statements about a business's products or services that cause it to lose money. Also called trade libel.
LAW-05.Misappropriation of likeness: Using a person's name, photo or identity for commercial gain, such as in an advertisement, without permission.
LAW-05.Unfair competition: Dishonest business practices that harm a rival, such as passing off your goods as another company's.
LAW-05.Negligent hiring: An employer's failure to check a job applicant with reasonable care, when the unfit person hired later harms someone.
LAW-05.Bad faith: An insurance company's unreasonable refusal to pay or properly handle a valid claim from its own policyholder.

BA-05.Chief executive officer: The highest-ranking executive, responsible for the company's overall direction and results. The CEO reports to the board of directors.
BA-05.President: A top officer who usually oversees the running of the company. The title is often held by the chief executive or the second in command.
BA-05.Chief financial officer: The executive in charge of the company's money: financial planning, reporting, budgets and raising funds. Known as the CFO.
BA-05.Chief operating officer: The executive who runs the company's day-to-day operations, usually reporting directly to the chief executive. Known as the COO.
BA-05.Vice president: A senior executive who heads a major function or division, such as sales or manufacturing, and ranks below the president.
BA-05.Chief marketing officer: The executive responsible for marketing, including advertising, branding and market research. Known as the CMO.
BA-05.Chief technology officer: The executive in charge of the technology the company develops and uses in its products. Known as the CTO.
BA-05.Chairman of the board: The person who leads the board of directors, the group elected by shareholders to oversee the company and its top managers.
BA-05.Managing director: The title used in the United Kingdom and many other countries for the executive who runs the company, similar to a chief executive.
BA-05.Chief information officer: The executive in charge of the company's internal computer systems and information technology strategy. Known as the CIO.
BA-05.Chief human resources officer: The executive responsible for hiring, training, pay, benefits and employee relations across the company.
BA-05.Treasurer: The officer who manages the company's cash, banking, borrowing and investments.
BA-05.Chief administrative officer: The executive who oversees the internal support functions that keep the company running, such as human resources and office services.
BA-05.Chief strategy officer: The executive who helps the chief executive develop long-term plans and makes sure they are carried out.
BA-05.Chief product officer: The executive responsible for deciding which products the company builds and for how they are developed and improved.
BA-05.Chief revenue officer: The executive responsible for everything that brings in income, usually overseeing sales, marketing and customer accounts.
BA-05.General counsel: The company's top lawyer, who heads the legal department and advises executives and the board on legal matters.
BA-05.Corporate secretary: The officer who keeps the corporation's official records, including minutes of board and shareholder meetings, and sees that legal filings are made.
BA-05.Controller: The company's chief accountant, who oversees the accounting records and the preparation of financial statements.
BA-05.Chief information security officer: The executive responsible for protecting the company's data and computer systems from attack and theft.
BA-05.Chief compliance officer: The executive who makes sure the company follows the laws, regulations and internal policies that apply to it.
BA-05.Chief sustainability officer: The executive who leads the company's efforts to reduce its environmental impact and meet its social responsibility goals.
BA-05.Chief diversity officer: The executive who leads efforts to build a workforce and workplace that include and treat fairly people of all backgrounds.
BA-05.Chief data officer: The executive responsible for how the company collects, manages, protects and uses its data.
BA-05.Chief risk officer: The executive who identifies and manages the major risks facing the company, such as financial, legal and safety risks.
BA-05.Chief accounting officer: The executive responsible for the company's accounting and for the accuracy of its financial reports.
BA-05.Chief investment officer: The executive who manages an organization's investment portfolio, common at banks, insurers and investment funds.
BA-05.Chief customer officer: The executive responsible for the overall experience customers have with the company and for keeping them satisfied.

BA-06.Strong passwords: Long passwords that mix letters, numbers and symbols, are hard to guess and are not reused across accounts.
BA-06.Antivirus software: A program that scans computers for viruses and other malicious software and blocks or removes them.
BA-06.Firewall: Hardware or software that sits between a company's network and the internet and blocks traffic that does not meet its security rules.
BA-06.Data backups: Extra copies of important files kept in a separate place, so the data can be restored after a loss, failure or attack.
BA-06.Encryption: Scrambling data into a code that can be read only by someone who has the key, so stolen data is useless to a thief.
BA-06.Multi-factor authentication: Requiring two or more proofs of identity to log in, such as a password plus a code sent to a phone.
BA-06.Employee training: Teaching staff to recognize threats such as phishing emails and to follow safe habits, since many breaches start with human error.
BA-06.Software updates: Installing the latest versions and patches for programs, which fix security holes that attackers could otherwise use.
BA-06.Access controls: Limits that let each user see and change only the data and systems needed for that person's job.
BA-06.Virtual private network: A tool that creates an encrypted connection over the internet, so remote employees can reach company systems safely. Known as a VPN.
BA-06.Security policies: Written rules for how employees must use and protect company computers, data and devices.
BA-06.Email filtering: Software that checks incoming email and blocks spam, phishing attempts and dangerous attachments before they reach users.
BA-06.Biometrics: Identifying a person by a physical trait, such as a fingerprint or face scan, in place of or in addition to a password.
BA-06.Physical security: Protecting the equipment itself with locked server rooms, key cards, cameras and guards, so that nobody can reach or steal it.
BA-06.Security audits: Reviews and tests of the company's systems, including hiring experts to try to break in, to find weaknesses before criminals do.
BA-06.Disaster recovery plan: A written plan for restoring computer systems and data and getting back to work after an attack, outage or natural disaster.
BA-06.Monitoring and activity logs: Watching systems and keeping records of who did what and when, so that unusual activity can be spotted and investigated.
BA-06.Secure data disposal: Destroying data that is no longer needed, by shredding paper and wiping or destroying old drives, so it cannot be recovered.
BA-06.Cloud security: Storing data with a cloud provider that protects it with safeguards such as encryption, backups and guarded data centers.
BA-06.Hiring IT security staff: Employing information technology specialists, or an outside security firm, whose job is to defend the company's systems.
BA-06.Cyber insurance: An insurance policy that helps pay the costs of a data breach or cyberattack, such as recovery, legal fees and notifying customers.
BA-06.Intrusion detection system: Software or a device that watches a network for signs of an attack or break-in and alerts the security team.
BA-06.Data loss prevention: Tools that detect and block sensitive information, such as customer records, from being sent or copied outside the company.
BA-06.Network segmentation: Dividing a network into separate sections so that an attacker who gets into one part cannot easily reach the rest.
BA-06.Zero trust security: An approach that trusts no user or device by default, even inside the network, and checks identity for every request.
BA-06.Tokenization: Replacing sensitive data, such as a card number, with a random stand-in value that is useless if stolen.
BA-06.Mobile device management: Software that lets a company enforce security rules on employees' phones and laptops and erase them remotely if lost.
BA-06.Uninterruptible power supply: A battery unit that keeps computers running for a short time when the power fails, preventing data loss and damage.
BA-06.Single sign-on: A system that lets a user log in once to reach many applications, which means fewer passwords to manage and protect.
BA-06.Data minimization: Collecting and keeping only the data the business truly needs, so there is less to be stolen in a breach.

POB-06.Economic conditions: The state of the economy, including inflation, interest rates, unemployment and whether it is growing or in recession, which affects how much customers spend.
POB-06.Competition: What rival businesses do, such as cutting prices, launching products or entering the market, which a firm can answer but not control.
POB-06.Technology: New inventions and methods that can make a firm's products or processes outdated, or open up new opportunities.
POB-06.Laws and regulations: Rules made by government that a business must obey, covering areas such as wages, safety, advertising and the environment.
POB-06.Political forces: The actions and stability of governments, including elections and changes in policy, which shape the climate for business.
POB-06.Social and cultural trends: Changes in people's values, lifestyles and tastes, such as a growing interest in healthy eating, that shift what customers want.
POB-06.Demographics: The makeup of the population, such as age, income, education and household size, and how it is changing.
POB-06.Natural environment: Weather, climate, natural disasters and the supply of natural resources, all of which can disrupt operations or change demand.
POB-06.Customer demand: How much of a product customers want to buy. A business can try to influence it but cannot decide it.
POB-06.Taxes: The rates and rules set by government for taxing income, sales and property, which change a firm's costs and customers' spending power.
POB-06.Global forces: Events and conditions beyond the home country, such as exchange rates, trade agreements, tariffs and wars.
POB-06.Suppliers: The firms that provide materials and goods. Their prices, reliability and shortages are outside the buying company's control.
POB-06.Labor market: The supply of available workers and the wages they expect, which affects how easily and cheaply a firm can hire.
POB-06.Substitute products: Different products that meet the same need, such as streaming in place of movie theaters, and can draw customers away.
POB-06.Ethical expectations: Society's standards for what counts as right and fair behavior by a business, which often go beyond what the law requires.
POB-06.Public opinion: What the public, the media and interest groups think and say about a company or its industry, which can help or hurt its reputation.
POB-06.Financial markets: Conditions in stock and credit markets, which decide how easily and at what cost a business can raise money.
POB-06.Energy prices and infrastructure: The cost of fuel and power, and the quality of roads, ports and internet networks that a business depends on but does not own.

POB-07.Charitable donations: Giving money, products or other resources to charities and good causes. Also called corporate philanthropy.
POB-07.Recycling: Collecting used materials such as paper, plastic and metal so they can be made into new products instead of becoming trash.
POB-07.Employee volunteering: Encouraging staff to give their time to community projects, sometimes with paid days off to do it.
POB-07.Reducing pollution: Cutting the harmful emissions and waste the business releases into the air, water and land.
POB-07.Fair wages: Paying employees enough to live on and in line with the value of their work, not merely the legal minimum.
POB-07.Community sponsorships: Paying to support local teams, events and programs, such as a youth sports league or a town festival.
POB-07.Renewable energy: Powering operations with sources that do not run out and pollute little, such as solar and wind.
POB-07.Conserving energy and water: Using less electricity, fuel and water, for example with efficient lighting and equipment, to lower the firm's environmental impact.
POB-07.Sustainable packaging: Packaging that uses less material or is recyclable, reusable or compostable, so it creates less waste.
POB-07.Ethical sourcing: Buying from suppliers that treat workers fairly and protect the environment, for example by choosing fair trade goods.
POB-07.Safe working conditions: Protecting employees from injury and illness at work through safe equipment, training and procedures.
POB-07.Diversity and inclusion: Hiring and promoting people of all backgrounds fairly and making sure everyone feels respected and able to contribute.
POB-07.Buying local: Purchasing supplies from nearby businesses and hiring local people, which keeps money and jobs in the community.
POB-07.Honest advertising: Telling the truth about products and prices and avoiding claims that could mislead customers.
POB-07.Safe products: Making sure products will not harm the people who use them, and recalling quickly any that turn out to be unsafe.
POB-07.Scholarships: Paying part of students' education costs or otherwise supporting schools and job training in the community.
POB-07.Tree planting: Planting trees or organizing cleanups to restore natural areas and offset some of the firm's environmental impact.
POB-07.Employee wellness programs: Programs that support employees' physical and mental health, such as fitness benefits, counseling and a healthy balance of work and life.
POB-07.Disaster relief: Giving money, supplies or services to help people and communities recover after events such as hurricanes and floods.
POB-07.Protecting customer privacy: Keeping customers' personal information secure and not selling or using it in ways they have not agreed to.
POB-07.Animal welfare: Avoiding cruelty to animals, for example by not testing products on them and by requiring humane treatment from suppliers.
POB-07.Cause marketing: A partnership in which a business ties its sales to a good cause, for example by donating a set amount to a charity for each item sold.
POB-07.Corporate foundation: A separate charitable organization set up and funded by a company to make grants. Many also match the donations employees make.
POB-07.Sustainability reporting: Publishing a regular report on the company's environmental and social performance, so the public can judge its record.
POB-07.B Corp certification: A certification from the nonprofit B Lab for companies that meet high standards of social and environmental performance, accountability and transparency.
POB-07.Pro bono work: Providing professional services free of charge to people or nonprofits that could not otherwise afford them.
POB-07.Hiring from underserved groups: Making a point of employing people who often struggle to find work, such as veterans, people with disabilities or people with a criminal record.
POB-07.Impact investing: Investing money in projects or businesses that aim to do social or environmental good as well as earn a financial return.
POB-07.Product take-back programs: Accepting customers' old products back at the end of their life so they can be recycled or disposed of safely.

HRM-05.Salary: A fixed amount of pay for a year of work, paid in regular installments regardless of the exact hours worked.
HRM-05.Hourly wage: Pay set at a fixed amount for each hour worked, so total pay rises and falls with the hours.
HRM-05.Commission: Pay calculated as a percentage of the sales an employee makes, common for salespeople.
HRM-05.Bonus: An extra payment on top of regular pay, given for reaching a goal, for strong results or at a special time such as year end.
HRM-05.Overtime pay: A higher pay rate for hours worked beyond the standard week. Federal law requires at least one and a half times regular pay for most hourly workers after 40 hours.
HRM-05.Tips: Money that customers give directly to service workers, such as restaurant servers, in thanks for good service.
HRM-05.Raise: An increase in an employee's regular rate of pay, given for good work, longer service or to keep up with the cost of living.
HRM-05.Salary plus commission: A pay plan that combines a guaranteed base salary with a percentage of sales, giving both security and an incentive.
HRM-05.Profit sharing: A plan in which the company pays employees a share of its profits, so they earn more when the business does well.
HRM-05.Stock options: The right to buy company shares at a fixed price in the future. They gain value if the share price rises above that price.
HRM-05.Merit pay: A pay increase awarded on the basis of how well an employee performed, as rated in a performance review.
HRM-05.Piece rate: Pay of a set amount for each unit an employee produces or task completed, so faster workers earn more.
HRM-05.Daily rate: Pay set at a fixed amount for each day worked, whatever the number of hours. Common for temporary and freelance work.
HRM-05.Contract or project fee: A set amount paid for completing a whole job or project, typical for freelancers and independent contractors.
HRM-05.Skill-based pay: A system that pays employees more for each additional job skill or qualification they master, not for the position they hold.
HRM-05.Shift differential: Extra pay per hour for working less popular shifts, such as nights, weekends or holidays.
HRM-05.Gainsharing: A group plan that pays employees a share of the money saved when their unit raises productivity or cuts costs.
HRM-05.Hazard pay: Extra pay for doing work that is dangerous or involves physical hardship.
HRM-05.Draw against commission: An advance paid to a salesperson at regular intervals, which is then subtracted from the commissions the person earns later.
HRM-05.On-call pay: Pay for the time an employee must stay available to come in or respond if needed, even when no work is done.
HRM-05.Sales spiff: A small, immediate bonus paid to a salesperson for selling a particular product, often funded by the product's maker.

HRM-06.Strike: Union members refuse to work until their demands are met. It is the union's strongest weapon, because it stops the employer's production.
HRM-06.Collective bargaining: The process in which union representatives and management negotiate a contract covering pay, hours, benefits and working conditions.
HRM-06.Picketing: Union members walk outside the workplace carrying signs, to tell the public about the dispute and discourage people from going in.
HRM-06.Boycott: The union urges its members and the public not to buy the employer's products, to put pressure on the company through lost sales.
HRM-06.Mediation: A neutral third party helps the two sides talk and suggests solutions, but has no power to force them to agree.
HRM-06.Compromise: Each side gives up some of what it wanted so that an agreement can be reached. Giving ground this way is called making concessions.
HRM-06.Arbitration: A neutral third party hears both sides and makes a decision. In binding arbitration, both sides must accept it.
HRM-06.Lockout: The employer closes the workplace or refuses to let union employees work, to pressure the union to accept its terms.
HRM-06.Grievance procedure: The step-by-step process set out in a union contract for handling an employee's complaint that the contract has been broken.
HRM-06.Strike vote: A vote in which union members decide whether to authorize a strike. A yes vote strengthens the union's hand in bargaining.
HRM-06.Layoffs: The employer cuts jobs, or threatens to close or move a plant, which puts pressure on the union to lower its demands.
HRM-06.Hiring replacement workers: The employer brings in other people to do the jobs of striking workers so the business can keep running. Strikers call them strikebreakers.
HRM-06.Injunction: A court order that requires a party to stop doing something, such as an illegal strike or violent picketing.
HRM-06.Work slowdown: Employees stay on the job but deliberately work more slowly or do only the minimum the rules require, to pressure the employer.
HRM-06.Union organizing drive: A campaign to sign up workers and win an election so that a union can represent them in dealing with the employer.
HRM-06.Fact-finding: A neutral third party investigates a dispute and issues a public report with recommendations, which the sides are not required to accept.
HRM-06.Collective bargaining agreement: The written contract that results from bargaining, setting pay, benefits and work rules for a fixed period. Members usually vote to approve it.
HRM-06.Lobbying: Unions and employers both try to persuade lawmakers to pass laws that favor their side.
HRM-06.Publicity campaign: Using advertising, news coverage and social media to win public sympathy for one side of a labor dispute.
HRM-06.Unfair labor practice charge: A formal complaint to the National Labor Relations Board that an employer or union has broken labor law, for example by firing a worker for union activity.
HRM-06.Sickout: Many employees call in sick on the same day as an organized protest, often used by workers who are not legally allowed to strike.
HRM-06.Decertification: A vote by employees to remove a union as their official bargaining representative.
HRM-06.Cooling-off period: A delay before a strike can go ahead. Under the Taft-Hartley Act, a court can order 80 days when a strike would endanger national health or safety.
HRM-06.Mutual aid pact: An agreement among employers in an industry to support one another financially if one of them is hit by a strike.
HRM-06.Strike fund: Money a union saves from members' dues to pay striking workers a small income while they are off the job.
HRM-06.Captive audience meeting: A meeting held on work time that employees are required to attend, at which the employer argues against joining a union.
HRM-06.Yellow-dog contract: An agreement in which a worker promises, as a condition of being hired, not to join a union. Federal law made such contracts unenforceable in 1932.
HRM-06.Sit-down strike: Strikers stop working but stay inside the workplace, which keeps the employer from bringing in replacements. U.S. labor law does not protect it, so strikers can be fired.
HRM-06.Interest-based bargaining: A cooperative style of negotiation in which both sides look for solutions that meet their shared and separate interests instead of trading fixed demands.

OPM-05.Price: What the supplier charges for the goods. A lower price raises the buyer's profit, but only if quality and service hold up.
OPM-05.Quality: How well the supplier's goods meet the buyer's standards. Poor materials lead to poor products and unhappy customers.
OPM-05.Delivery speed: How quickly an order arrives after it is placed. The gap between ordering and receiving is called lead time.
OPM-05.Reliability: Whether the supplier consistently delivers the right goods, in the right quantity, on the promised date.
OPM-05.Location: How near the supplier is. A closer supplier usually means faster delivery, lower freight costs and easier communication.
OPM-05.Customer service: How well the supplier communicates, answers questions and fixes problems before and after the sale.
OPM-05.Reputation: What other buyers say about the supplier and its track record in the industry.
OPM-05.Shipping costs: What it costs to transport the goods from the supplier. A low price can be wiped out by high freight charges.
OPM-05.Product selection: The range of items the supplier carries. A wide selection lets a buyer get more of what it needs from one source.
OPM-05.Payment terms: The conditions for paying, such as how many days the buyer has before the bill is due and whether credit is offered.
OPM-05.Discounts: Price reductions the supplier offers, for example for buying in large quantities or for paying the bill early.
OPM-05.Flexibility: The supplier's willingness to handle rush orders, changes in quantity and special or customized requests.
OPM-05.Contract terms: The conditions of the agreement, such as how long it lasts, whether it is exclusive and how it can be ended.
OPM-05.Capacity: Whether the supplier can produce or stock enough to fill the buyer's orders, including when demand grows.
OPM-05.Return policy: The rules for sending back defective or unsold goods, along with any warranty or guarantee the supplier gives.
OPM-05.Minimum order quantity: The smallest amount the supplier will sell in one order. A high minimum can force a small business to buy more than it needs.
OPM-05.Technology: Whether the supplier's ordering and tracking systems are easy to use and work with the buyer's own systems.
OPM-05.Expertise: The supplier's knowledge of its products and the industry, which lets it give useful advice and solve technical problems.
OPM-05.Certifications: Proof from an outside body that the supplier meets recognized standards for quality, safety or legal requirements.
OPM-05.Financial stability: Whether the supplier is financially healthy enough to stay in business and keep filling orders in the long run.
OPM-05.Ethical practices: Whether the supplier treats its workers fairly and limits harm to the environment, since its conduct reflects on the buyer.
OPM-05.Risk of supply disruption: The chance that deliveries will be cut off by events such as disasters, strikes or political trouble where the supplier operates.
OPM-05.Tariffs and import costs: The taxes, customs fees and currency exchange costs that are added when buying from a supplier in another country.
OPM-05.Promotional support: Help the supplier gives the buyer in selling its goods, such as sharing advertising costs, displays or staff training.
OPM-05.Cultural fit: How well the supplier's values and ways of working match the buyer's, which matters for a long-term partnership.
OPM-05.Diversity status: Whether the supplier is owned by a group such as minorities, women or veterans. Some buyers set goals for buying from such firms.

OPM-06.Slips, trips and falls: Falls caused by wet or slippery floors, loose cords, clutter or uneven surfaces. They are among the most common workplace injuries.
OPM-06.Fire: The danger of fire or explosion from flammable liquids, gas leaks, combustible dust or faulty equipment.
OPM-06.Hazardous chemicals: Substances that can burn, poison or sicken workers who touch or breathe them, such as cleaning agents, solvents and fumes.
OPM-06.Electrical hazards: Exposed wires, damaged cords and overloaded outlets that can cause electric shock, burns or fires.
OPM-06.Dangerous machinery: Equipment with moving parts that can catch, crush or cut a worker, especially when safety guards are missing or broken.
OPM-06.Heavy lifting: Lifting or carrying heavy loads, or lifting the wrong way, which strains the back and muscles.
OPM-06.Sharp objects: Knives, blades, box cutters, needles and broken glass that can cut or puncture the skin.
OPM-06.Hot surfaces and burns: Stoves, fryers, steam and hot liquids that can burn or scald workers, common in kitchens and factories.
OPM-06.Loud noise: Constant or very loud sound, for example from machinery, that can permanently damage hearing over time.
OPM-06.Working at heights: Work on ladders, scaffolds or roofs, where a fall can cause serious injury or death.
OPM-06.Falling objects or moving vehicles: The danger of being struck, for example by items falling from shelves or by forklifts and trucks moving around the workplace.
OPM-06.Lack of safety training: Workers who have not been taught the safe way to do a job are more likely to make mistakes that injure themselves or others.
OPM-06.Missing protective equipment: Working without the gear the job needs, such as gloves, goggles, hard hats or masks, leaves workers exposed to injury.
OPM-06.Poor lighting: Dim or uneven light that makes it hard to see obstacles and hazards, leading to trips, errors and eye strain.
OPM-06.Repetitive motion: Doing the same movement over and over, or working in an awkward position, which slowly injures muscles, tendons and nerves. It is an ergonomic hazard.
OPM-06.Extreme temperatures: Working in very hot or very cold conditions, which can cause heat stroke, dehydration, frostbite or hypothermia.
OPM-06.Workplace violence: Threats or physical attacks at work, from robbers, angry customers or coworkers.
OPM-06.Blocked exits: Doors, aisles and walkways obstructed by boxes or clutter, which can trap people in an emergency and cause trips.
OPM-06.Confined spaces: Tight enclosed areas such as tanks, tunnels and trenches, where air can run short, toxic gas can collect or walls can cave in.
OPM-06.Radiation: Exposure to harmful energy such as X-rays, radioactive materials or strong ultraviolet light from the sun.
OPM-06.Compressed gas and pressure: Cylinders, boilers and other pressurized containers that can leak, burst or explode if damaged or mishandled.
OPM-06.Biological hazards: Living things that can make workers ill, such as bacteria, viruses, mold and blood carrying disease.
OPM-06.Fatigue: Tiredness from long hours, too little rest or heavy stress, which slows reactions and leads to mistakes and accidents.
OPM-06.Vibration: Shaking from power tools or heavy vehicles that, over time, can damage nerves, blood vessels and joints.
OPM-06.Drug or alcohol impairment: A worker under the influence of drugs or alcohol has poor judgment and slow reactions, endangering everyone nearby.
OPM-06.Structural hazards: Parts of the building that are damaged or unstable, such as broken stairs, missing handrails or weak floors and shelving.
OPM-06.Lack of emergency preparedness: Having no evacuation plan, fire extinguishers, smoke detectors or first aid supplies, which makes any emergency far more dangerous.

BCM-05.Slides: Screens of brief text and images, made in a program such as PowerPoint, projected behind the speaker to show the key points.
BCM-05.Charts and graphs: Drawings that turn numbers into pictures, such as bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts, so the audience can see trends and comparisons quickly.
BCM-05.Video: A short film clip played during the talk to show something in action or to add interest and emotion.
BCM-05.Handouts: Printed pages given to the audience with details, data or a summary that they can follow and take away.
BCM-05.Poster: A large printed or hand-made sheet or board that displays the main ideas with text and pictures.
BCM-05.Photographs: Pictures that show the audience what a real person, place or product looks like.
BCM-05.Whiteboard: A board the speaker writes or draws on during the talk, good for working through ideas live with the audience.
BCM-05.Props: Physical objects the speaker shows or passes around, such as a product sample, so the audience sees the real thing.
BCM-05.Flip chart: A large pad of paper on an easel. The speaker writes on a sheet and flips it over to continue on the next.
BCM-05.Demonstration: Showing the audience how something works by actually doing it or using the product in front of them.
BCM-05.Table: Information arranged in rows and columns, useful for showing exact figures or comparing options side by side.
BCM-05.Website or app demo: Showing a live website or application on screen so the audience can watch how it works.
BCM-05.Diagram: A simplified drawing that shows the parts of something or how a process works, such as a flowchart or an organizational chart.
BCM-05.Map: A drawing of an area that shows where places are, such as store locations, sales territories or delivery routes.
BCM-05.Model: A three-dimensional copy of an object, often smaller than the real thing, such as a scale model of a building or a product prototype.
BCM-05.Timeline: A line marked with dates that shows events or project steps in the order they happen.
BCM-05.Infographic: A single graphic that combines pictures, icons, numbers and a few words to explain a topic at a glance.
BCM-05.Document camera: A camera on a stand that projects a live image of a paper page or small object onto a screen for the whole room to see.
BCM-05.Virtual or augmented reality: Virtual reality places viewers in a computer-made 3D world through a headset. Augmented reality adds digital images to a live view of the real world.
BCM-05.Word cloud: An image made of words in which the words used most often appear largest, showing the main themes of a text or survey.
BCM-05.Sample portfolio: A binder or folder of work examples or product samples that the speaker shows to the audience as evidence.

BCM-06.Sender: The person or organization that has an idea to share and starts the communication.
BCM-06.Receiver: The person or audience the message is aimed at, who takes it in and works out its meaning.
BCM-06.Message: The idea, information or feeling that the sender wants the receiver to understand.
BCM-06.Feedback: The receiver's response, in words or actions, which shows the sender whether the message was understood as intended.
BCM-06.Channel: The route by which a message travels from sender to receiver, such as a face-to-face talk, a phone call, an email or a letter.
BCM-06.Noise: Anything that interferes with a message and keeps it from being received as sent, from loud sounds to a distracted mind.
BCM-06.Encoding: The sender's step of turning an idea into words, pictures, gestures or other symbols that can be sent.
BCM-06.Decoding: The receiver's step of interpreting the words or symbols received and working out what the sender meant.
BCM-06.Context: The setting and circumstances in which communication takes place, which shape how a message is sent and understood.
BCM-06.Frame of reference: The background, experience and beliefs each person brings to a conversation. The more two people share, the more easily they understand each other.

BMA-06.SWOT analysis: A review of a business's internal Strengths and Weaknesses and its external Opportunities and Threats.
BMA-06.Mission statement: A short statement of the organization's purpose, which guides its goals and decisions. A vision statement describes what it hopes to become.
BMA-06.SMART goals: Goals written to be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, so progress can be checked.
BMA-06.Budget: A financial plan that sets out expected income and spending for a period and puts the strategy into numbers.
BMA-06.Business plan: A written document that describes the business, its goals and market, and how it will reach those goals.
BMA-06.Competitive analysis: A study of rival businesses, including their products, prices, strengths and weaknesses, to find where the company can gain an edge.
BMA-06.PEST analysis: A scan of the Political, Economic, Social and Technological forces outside the business that could affect it.
BMA-06.Key performance indicators: A small set of measurable figures, such as sales growth or customer retention, used to track progress toward strategic goals. Known as KPIs.
BMA-06.Market research: Gathering and analyzing information about customers, competitors and the market to guide decisions.
BMA-06.Forecasting: Using past data and trends to predict future figures such as sales, costs or demand.
BMA-06.Benchmarking: Comparing the company's performance and practices with those of the best in the industry to find where it can improve.
BMA-06.Porter five forces: Michael Porter's model for judging how competitive an industry is, based on rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power.
BMA-06.Break-even analysis: A calculation of the sales level at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
BMA-06.Cost-benefit analysis: Adding up the expected costs of a decision and comparing them with its expected benefits to see if it is worthwhile.
BMA-06.Management by objectives: A process in which managers and employees agree on goals that support the company's strategy and then review results against them.
BMA-06.Brainstorming: A group session for producing as many ideas as possible, without criticism, before sorting out the best ones.
BMA-06.BCG matrix: The Boston Consulting Group's grid that sorts a company's products by market growth and market share into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.
BMA-06.Balanced scorecard: A system that measures performance from four views: financial, customer, internal processes, and learning and growth.
BMA-06.Scenario planning: Imagining several different ways the future could unfold and planning how the business would respond to each.
BMA-06.Objectives and key results: A goal-setting system that pairs each objective with a few measurable results that show whether it has been achieved. Known as OKRs.
BMA-06.Core competency analysis: Identifying what the company does especially well and competitors find hard to copy, so strategy can be built on it.
BMA-06.Strategy map: A one-page diagram that shows how a company's objectives link together by cause and effect to produce its overall goals.
BMA-06.Decision tree: A branching diagram that lays out the choices available, the possible outcomes of each and their likely payoffs.
BMA-06.Product life cycle: A model of the stages a product passes through, namely introduction, growth, maturity and decline, each of which calls for a different strategy.
BMA-06.Ansoff matrix: A grid of four growth strategies based on new or existing products and markets: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification.
BMA-06.Value chain analysis: Michael Porter's method of examining each activity a company performs, from buying materials to after-sale service, to see where value is added.
BMA-06.Gap analysis: Comparing where the business is now with where it wants to be, then working out the steps needed to close the difference.
BMA-06.VRIO framework: A test of whether a resource gives lasting advantage: is it Valuable, Rare, hard to Imitate and is the firm Organized to use it?
BMA-06.McKinsey 7S framework: A model for checking that seven parts of an organization fit together: strategy, structure, systems, shared values, skills, style and staff.
BMA-06.GE-McKinsey matrix: A nine-box grid that rates each business unit on industry attractiveness and its own competitive strength, to decide where to invest.
BMA-06.Blue ocean strategy: The idea of creating a new market space with no direct rivals instead of fighting competitors in a crowded existing market.
BMA-06.Porter generic strategies: Michael Porter's three basic ways to compete: cost leadership, differentiation, or focus on a narrow market segment.
BMA-06.Hoshin kanri: A Japanese planning method that passes a few top strategic goals down through every level so that daily work lines up with them.
BMA-06.TOWS matrix: An extension of SWOT that pairs external opportunities and threats with internal strengths and weaknesses to produce specific strategies.
BMA-06.Business model canvas: A one-page chart with nine blocks that describe how a business creates, delivers and earns from value, including customers, costs and revenue.
BMA-06.SOAR analysis: A positive-focused planning tool that looks at Strengths, Opportunities, Aspirations and Results.
BMA-06.Stakeholder analysis: Identifying the people and groups affected by a strategy and weighing their interests and influence.

BMA-07.Leader: An interpersonal role. The manager directs, motivates, trains and develops the people in the unit.
BMA-07.Negotiator: A decisional role. The manager represents the organization in bargaining, for example with suppliers, unions or customers.
BMA-07.Spokesperson: An informational role. The manager speaks for the organization, passing information about it to people outside.
BMA-07.Entrepreneur: A decisional role. The manager looks for opportunities and starts projects that change and improve the organization.
BMA-07.Monitor: An informational role. The manager seeks out and collects information from inside and outside the organization to stay aware of what is happening.
BMA-07.Resource allocator: A decisional role. The manager decides who gets the organization's money, people, equipment and time.
BMA-07.Disturbance handler: A decisional role. The manager deals with unexpected problems and crises, such as a conflict between staff or the loss of a major customer.
BMA-07.Liaison: An interpersonal role. The manager builds and keeps up a network of contacts outside the unit, inside and outside the organization.
BMA-07.Figurehead: An interpersonal role. The manager performs ceremonial and symbolic duties, such as signing documents and greeting visitors.
BMA-07.Disseminator: An informational role. The manager passes useful information on to the people inside the organization who need it.

LAW-06.Employment contract: An agreement between an employer and an employee that sets out the job, pay, benefits and conditions for ending the employment.
LAW-06.Lease: A contract that gives a business the right to use property, such as a store, office or equipment, for a set time in return for rent.
LAW-06.Sales contract: An agreement in which a seller promises to hand over goods or services and a buyer promises to pay a stated price.
LAW-06.Loan agreement: A contract in which a lender provides money and the borrower promises to repay it with interest on agreed terms.
LAW-06.Non-disclosure agreement: A contract in which the signer promises to keep certain information confidential and not share it with others. Known as an NDA.
LAW-06.Partnership agreement: A contract among the co-owners of a partnership stating each partner's investment, duties, share of profits and what happens if one leaves.
LAW-06.Franchise agreement: A contract that lets a franchisee run a business under the franchisor's name and system in return for fees and royalties.
LAW-06.Supplier contract: An agreement with a vendor that sets the price, quantity, quality and delivery terms for the goods it will provide.
LAW-06.Insurance policy: A contract in which an insurer, in return for premium payments, agrees to pay for specified losses if they occur.
LAW-06.Service contract: An agreement for one party to perform work for another, such as cleaning, maintenance or consulting, for a stated fee.
LAW-06.Non-compete agreement: A contract in which an employee or seller of a business promises not to work for or start a competing business for a set time and area. Some states limit or ban them for employees.
LAW-06.Warranty: A seller's promise that a product will meet certain standards, and that it will be repaired or replaced if it does not.
LAW-06.Real estate purchase contract: A written agreement to buy land or a building, stating the price and conditions. Contracts for real estate must be in writing.
LAW-06.Licensing agreement: A contract in which the owner of a patent, trademark, copyright or software lets another party use it, usually in return for a fee or royalty.
LAW-06.Independent contractor agreement: A contract with a self-employed person or firm hired for a specific job, who is not an employee of the business.
LAW-06.Shareholder agreement: A contract among a company's owners covering their rights and duties, such as voting, selling shares and settling disputes.
LAW-06.Merger or acquisition agreement: The contract under which two companies combine, or one buys another, stating the price and terms of the deal.
LAW-06.Sponsorship agreement: A contract in which a business pays to support an event, team or person in exchange for publicity for its brand.
LAW-06.Shipping contract: An agreement with a carrier to transport goods, stating the price, the route and who is responsible for loss or damage.
LAW-06.Settlement agreement: A contract that ends a legal dispute without a trial, usually with one side paying and the other giving up the right to sue.
LAW-06.Collective bargaining agreement: The contract between an employer and a labor union that sets pay, hours, benefits and working conditions for the union's members.
LAW-06.Joint venture agreement: A contract in which two or more businesses agree to work together on one specific project, sharing its costs, control and profits.
LAW-06.Terms of service: The rules a customer must accept in order to use a company's website, app or service.
LAW-06.Memorandum of understanding: A written outline of what two parties intend to do together. It is often a step toward a formal contract and is usually not fully binding.
LAW-06.Consignment agreement: A contract under which a seller displays and sells goods that still belong to the supplier, keeping a share of each sale.
LAW-06.Indemnity agreement: A contract in which one party promises to cover the losses or legal claims another party may suffer.
LAW-06.Option contract: An agreement in which one party pays for the right to buy or sell something at a set price within a set time, without being obliged to.
LAW-06.Agency agreement: A contract that authorizes one party, the agent, to act and make deals on behalf of another, the principal.
LAW-06.Arbitration agreement: A contract, or a clause in one, in which the parties agree to settle any dispute through a private arbitrator instead of going to court.
LAW-06.Exclusive dealing agreement: A contract in which a buyer agrees to purchase only from one supplier, or a seller agrees to sell only through one dealer.
LAW-06.Assignment of intellectual property: A contract that transfers ownership of a creation, such as an invention or design, from one party to another, often from an employee to the employer.

ECO-07.NAFTA or USMCA: The North American Free Trade Agreement removed most tariffs among the United States, Canada and Mexico from 1994. The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement replaced it in 2020.
ECO-07.European Union: A political and economic union of 27 European countries with a single market in which goods, services, money and people move freely. Most members share the euro.
ECO-07.World Trade Organization: The global body, founded in 1995, that sets the rules of trade between nations and settles trade disputes among its members. Known as the WTO.
ECO-07.International Monetary Fund: An organization of about 190 countries that promotes stable exchange rates and lends to countries in financial crisis. Known as the IMF.
ECO-07.World Bank: An international organization that lends money and gives advice to developing countries for projects that reduce poverty, such as roads and schools.
ECO-07.OPEC: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Its members coordinate how much oil they produce, which influences world oil prices.
ECO-07.G7: The Group of Seven: a forum of seven large advanced economies whose leaders meet each year to discuss economic policy and world issues.
ECO-07.G20: The Group of Twenty: a forum of the world's major advanced and emerging economies that meets to coordinate global economic policy.
ECO-07.World Economic Forum: A nonprofit organization, best known for its yearly meeting in Davos, Switzerland, where business and political leaders discuss world issues.
ECO-07.ASEAN: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations: a group of Southeast Asian countries that promotes economic cooperation and free trade in the region.
ECO-07.GATT: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade: a 1947 agreement to cut tariffs and other trade barriers. It led to the World Trade Organization in 1995.
ECO-07.APEC: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation: a forum of economies around the Pacific Ocean that promotes free trade and investment in the region.
ECO-07.BRICS: A group of major emerging economies named for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, which has since added more members.
ECO-07.CAFTA-DR: A free trade agreement between the United States, five Central American countries and the Dominican Republic.
ECO-07.Regional development banks: International banks that lend for development projects in one part of the world, such as the Asian Development Bank and the African Development Bank.
ECO-07.Mercosur: A South American trade bloc, also called the Southern Common Market, founded by Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.
ECO-07.OECD: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development: a group of mostly wealthy democracies that compares policies and publishes economic data.
ECO-07.CPTPP: The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership: a free trade agreement among Pacific Rim countries such as Japan, Canada and Australia.
ECO-07.African Continental Free Trade Area: An agreement among most African countries to create one continent-wide market by cutting tariffs on trade between them.
ECO-07.RCEP: The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership: a free trade agreement among Asia-Pacific countries including China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the ASEAN members.
ECO-07.EFTA: The European Free Trade Association: a free trade group made up of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.
ECO-07.CARICOM: The Caribbean Community: a group of Caribbean countries that works toward a common market and coordinated economic policy.
ECO-07.ECOWAS: The Economic Community of West African States: a regional group that promotes trade and economic integration among West African countries.
ECO-07.Andean Community: A South American trade bloc made up of Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.
ECO-07.Gulf Cooperation Council: An economic and political union of six Arab states on the Persian Gulf, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
ECO-07.Pacific Alliance: A Latin American trade bloc formed by Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru to free up trade among themselves and with Asia.
ECO-07.COMESA: The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa: a free trade area of countries stretching from Egypt down to southern Africa.
ECO-07.SADC: The Southern African Development Community: a regional group of southern African countries that promotes trade and economic cooperation.
ECO-07.Eurasian Economic Union: An economic union of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia and Kyrgyzstan with a common market among its members.
ECO-07.SAARC: The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation: a group of South Asian countries, including India and Pakistan, that set up a regional free trade area.
ECO-07.Bank for International Settlements: An international institution based in Switzerland that serves as a bank for central banks and promotes global financial stability.
ECO-07.World Customs Organization: An international body that helps national customs services work together and maintains the standard system for classifying traded goods.
ECO-07.East African Community: A regional bloc of East African countries, including Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, with a customs union and common market.
ECO-07.UNCTAD: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development: a United Nations body that helps developing countries benefit from trade and investment.
